items.basis: The proposed mechanism relies on controlled mechanical stress to induce protective oxide layer formation, yet the cited evidence (doi:10.3323/jcorr1974.29.7_354) demonstrates that stress corrosion cracking of stainless steel in cooling water environments is a significant failure mode, making it impossible to reliably control stress below the cracking threshold while maintaining beneficial oxide formation.

The candidate fails to define critical boundary conditions including water chemistry parameters (pH, chloride concentration, temperature), flow rates, and stress application methods that would determine whether the mechanism succeeds or fails in a district cooling loop.

None of the cited evidence supports the proposed mechanism; instead, they address unrelated topics (heat transfer correlations, CO2-rich biogas combustion, boiling heat transfer, phase change materials), providing no scientific basis for the claimed stress-induced oxide layer formation.

The candidate provides no evidence that the proposed intervention would outperform the baseline, as the testable prediction only compares between stressed and unstressed plates without comparison to existing anti-fouling technologies or cleaning protocols.

Applying controlled mechanical stress to plate channels during operation in a functioning heat exchanger is mechanically infeasible without compromising structural integrity or requiring complete redesign of heat exchangers with integrated stress application systems.

The testable prediction fails to account for confounding variables such as seasonal variations in cooling water quality, biofilm composition changes over time, and the difficulty in isolating stress effects from other factors influencing heat transfer coefficients and pressure drops.
